research_tasks: Research log (2026-10-18, first run, mode create, empty baseline and no research notes). Opened 24 sources and failed to open 4 (S25-S28). Read in full: the Town & Country cover profile (S20), Vogue 2024 (S01), the Interview conversation with Sarah Paulson (S04), IndieWire on Act One (S06), Netflix Tudum (S11), Variety (S12), Collider (S13), the Netflix press-conference report (S14) and the Broadway Direct Q&A (S02); transcribed the 52-minute In The Moment podcast with local Whisper (S05, small.en for the whole episode, large-v3-turbo for the quoted passages) and read caption transcripts of ten video interviews dated May 2024 to September 26, 2026 (S03, S07, S08, S10, S13 video, S15-S19; about 11,000 words). Evidence was gathered before a type was chosen. Outcome: no defensible discriminator; the subject meets open-case eligibility (adult, first professional role January 2024, first lead September 2026, record made of promotional cycles plus friendly testimony). Status ready, profile_format open_case, leading read Type 6 at low confidence, Type 9 as the alternative, Types 2 and 3 live; Types 1 and 4 considered and set aside. Risks set: contested_typing (required for open cases) and sensitive_allegations (a TMZ insinuation about her friendship with Sarah Paulson, C29, and an anonymous 2018 Page Six item about her Juilliard admission, C30), so the six-role jury applies.

Accuracy check (2026-10-18). Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story premiered on Netflix on September 17, 2026, and was No. 1 on the global English TV list in its first two weeks (14.5 million views for September 21-27, S23). Act One premiered at Tribeca on June 10, 2026; a 2027 theatrical release via Oscilloscope was reported by one outlet but not opened. The Bell Jar (Sarah Polley; she plays Joan) has wrapped and has no announced release date. Town & Country (September 23, 2026) mentions an unannounced project she was shooting in Los Angeles. No new casting announcement dated October 2026 was found. The most recent interview located (Wonderland, October 5, 2026) could not be opened. open_case.next_review is 2026-12-15, after the Golden Globe nominations expected in December.

Drafting guidance (open case). Follow the standard's 'Open case profiles' section. Open with who she is and why people are searching (her first lead, Netflix's No. 1 show, the famous parents), then name the open question: what her steady humility and her named fear are for. Show what the record shows, dated and sourced, with limits: the auditions (C05, C06), the way she meets the inheritance question (C07, C08), duty and preparation (C10-C13, C33), the trusted circle (C16, C17), the luck register (C14, C31), the worry and self-trust passage (C32), the discomfort with being public (C15), and the composure others see (C18, C19). Set Type 6 beside Types 9, 2 and 3 with the best evidence for and against each. Include an H2 beginning '## What would settle it' built from open_case.settle_signals. Keep '## What is Ella Beatty's personality type?' with an answer of at most 60 words in 'leading read, held loosely' language, for example: 'Leading read: Type 6, held loosely. Type 9 is the live alternative, with 2 and 3 still in play.' Target 1,200 to 2,500 words. Titles, description and FAQs must say 'leading read' or 'open case', never 'is a Type 6'. Set enneagram: 6 and published: false. The strongest hook candidates are verified and specific: she was waiting at the Carlyle before the Vogue reporter, following her father's 'Always be on time' (S01); she won Monster from a self-tape among seven (S19); in the same year she played a daughter dragged away from acting by her parents and a daughter who kills hers, and said 'What is the universe saying? I don't know... I'm going to be examining that' (S20).

Quotation cautions. (a) S03, S07, S08, S10 (broadcast captions), S13 video, S15, S16, S17, S18 and S19 are YouTube caption transcripts without speaker labels; check each printed quote against the audio and timestamp. (b) S05 is a Whisper transcript without speaker labels; quoted passages were re-transcribed with large-v3-turbo (see the S05 context), but confirm speaker by listening. In particular, the lines 'how do I be what you want... How do I be beautiful enough for you? How do I be interesting enough for you?' (about 35:56-36:06) may be the host's; do not attribute them to her without checking. (c) Variety's 'I've never played a true out-and-out villain' is Rebecca Hall's, not Beatty's (S12). (d) Charlie Hunnam's 'one of the best actresses he'll ever work with' is the Entertainment Tonight interviewer's report, not Hunnam on record (S08). (e) The TODAY captions render 'female rage and representation'; Netflix's statement gives 'female rage and repression'; quote neither from the captions. (f2) In S05 the line about legacy as 'that thing of feeling rooted in something and grounded in something that's such a gift' (about 45:38-45:59) and the rehearsal joke 'the worst actor ever' (about 09:15) cannot be assigned to a speaker from the transcript; do not attribute them to her without listening. (f) The Broadway.com write-up lines ('I am who I am', 'She's why I'm who I am', 'There's definitely a privilege...') were obtained through a summarizing fetch and are not in the 7-minute video; verify before quoting. (g) WWD quotes (Gus Van Sant, the Feud notebook) are secondhand via Biography.com (S22). (h) The New York Times review line 'fulfill[ed] the play's plan perfectly' is quoted from Town & Country (S20); open the review before quoting it directly. (i) In the ScreenRant roundtable (S19) use the original English caption track; the alternate track is a machine translation. Speakers there: Beatty to about 03:05, Hunnam to about 06:55, Max Winkler after. (j) Ian Brennan's 'blank slate' and 'innocence' quotes come from an unopened TV Insider piece (S28); do not use.

Sensitivity. Never repeat, link or allude to the TMZ insinuation about Beatty and Sarah Paulson (C29, S24); describe the friendship only in the two women's own words. Do not use the 2018 Page Six admissions item (C30, S25) unless the original is opened, and then only as an attributed, unconfirmed gossip report with the context that she auditioned and completed the four-year program. Do not name or characterize her siblings. Do not read Lizzie Borden, or Act One's parents, into her family (the queue note says so explicitly); her account of her parents is warm and is the only account on record. Do not speculate about her parents' ages or health. No diagnosis-like language about anxiety: 'nervous', 'scared' and 'worry' are her words; keep them hers.

Follow-ups worth doing before or at the next refresh: (1) open the Forbes Q&A (S26), the Wonderland interview (S27) and the TV Insider piece with Ian Brennan's casting quotes (S28) from a different network or through a subscription; (2) find and open the WWD 2024 and 2025 interviews, the full Broadway.com Show People episode and the New York Times review of Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes; (3) listen to S05 at 23:15-26:00, 29:55-32:00 and 33:50-37:40 to confirm speaker attribution; (4) look for any long-form interview or podcast given after September 2026, and for Golden Globe or other awards-season interviews; (5) search for testimony from Juilliard faculty or classmates, or from the Ghosts company (Billy Crudup, Lily Rabe, Jack O'Brien); (6) if the Page Six original surfaces, record exactly what it claims and who it cites.

sources.locator: Full transcript (read through r.jina.ai). Intro paragraph (Paulson and Esper chose her; 'I had no idea who your parents were'); offer 'the next morning'; Paulson: 'self-possessed'; surname exchange ('It really never occurred to me until I started working... responsibility towards an artistic legacy'); 'Always, always' and make-believe; 'Appropriate really changed my life'; pressure answer ('responsibility to honor what the other actors are doing... I better show up'); Hugh Jackman and keeping 'awe'; closest character ('I am not a good liar. I have a hard time not being totally earnest'; 'It's a relief to come to work and remember you're being someone else'); her question to Paulson about 'tremendous care'; nights off ('I get really nervous', Ian Rickson's diary book).
sources.excerpt: “The pressure that I felt had to do with the responsibility to honor what the other actors are doing. You don’t want to leave people in the lurch. You want to show up and support people [...] I also felt like, ‘Okay, they’ve given me this job, so I better show up.’ I didn’t have a lot of time to be scared” [...] “I think her inability to not tell the truth is something I relate to. I am not a good liar. I have a hard time not being totally earnest.” [...] “Sometimes we have four or five days between performances and I get really nervous.”
sources.context: Long conversation recorded on Zoom in May 2025 during the Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes run. The interviewer is her close friend and former co-star, so this is both self-report and friendly testimony (Paulson: 'The thing that comes to mind most clearly is self-possessed'). The register is affectionate and joking ('my Venmo is...', astrology), which should be read as banter.

I try really hard and fail at often'; 'trusting yourself to have... the tools and the ability to handle it... is something I'm still really trying to do'); 33:50-35:00 (Feud; 'I can't believe they picked me'); 36:20-37:35 (auditions 'such a vulnerable, scary thing'; friends to call); 40:30-41:20 (Juilliard at 18, no professional career 'until I was like 22'); 45:40-47:10 (a line on legacy as 'feeling rooted in something and grounded in something' whose speaker is uncertain; her parents as different artists, her mother 'a real actor's actor'; 'I'm so lucky'); 50:35-51:10 (speed round: 'What scares you?' 'Everything. Ghosts. We'll leave it at that'; 'Take it a day at a time'; teaching theater to five- and six-year-olds).
sources.excerpt: “And being present and kind of being where your feet are, it's something I try to try really hard and fail at often frequently to live by. It's just like, you know, so much of what we worry about in life, so many of the things that we are so, so emotionally fraught about, you know, you can't handle until you're there. And I think trusting yourself to have, you know, the tools and the ability to handle it when you're faced with it is something I'm still really trying to do. And God knows that was something I did in that play.” [...] “I think because I felt that assurance from her going into it, I didn't feel a pressure to replicate anybody else's [...] you can't just come in and do whatever you want, but you serve the play” [...] “there's a part of me that feels like, Oh my God, I can't believe they picked me”
sources.context: The longest first-person source: a relaxed 52-minute conversation with Anthony Meindl, an acting teacher who calls her 'my dear friend', recorded early in 2025 while she was rehearsing Ghosts. The host talks at length and steers toward his podcast's theme of presence, so some of her statements extend his points. No speaker labels: the episode was transcribed locally with Whisper small.en, and the quoted passages were re-transcribed with large-v3-turbo; wording differences between the two runs are minor (for example 'helped' vs 'held me and supported me'; 'serve the plate' is Whisper's mishearing of 'serve the play'). Excerpts here omit fillers such as 'um'; restore them or mark the omission when quoting. Speaker attribution follows the conversational turns and should be confirmed by listening, especially around 35:56-36:06, where lines about trying to 'be what you want' may be the host's. Draft stage: quotations restore a mid-sentence 'um' where spoken and drop leading 'and, uh' and repeated false starts only at the start of a quotation; checked against the large-v3-turbo clips (clip_a, clip_b, clip_c, clip_h).

claims.claim: Vogue's reporter arrived at 2:58 p.m. for a 3 p.m. meeting at the Carlyle in February 2024 and found Beatty already there with her coat folded over her arm; Beatty was following her father's rule 'Always be on time' ('Or, in her case, early').

claims.inference: One observed instance, reported by the writer (S01). It shows reliability and pre-emptive care about expectations in a first major interview; the rule is her report of her father's advice.
claims.alternative: Punctuality for a Vogue interview is ordinary professionalism and a single occasion. 'In her case, early' paraphrases Taylor's own aside. The 'Be kind' and 'listen' rules from the same article are not used in the draft except 'listen' via TODAY (C56).

claims.claim: In February 2024 she raised the nepotism question before the Vogue reporter asked it ('without me even asking', per Taylor) and answered: 'I totally acknowledge that there is an inherent privilege and exposure that comes from having well-known actors as parents... And I really hope that I can offer something meaningful.'
claims.passage: Then, before Taylor could ask, Beatty raised the subject every story about her would raise. "I totally acknowledge that there is an inherent privilege and exposure that comes from having well-known actors as parents," she told [Vogue](https://www.vogue.com/article/meet-ella-beatty-the-breakout-star-of-feud-whos-now-heading-to-broadway). "And I really hope that I can offer something meaningful."
claims.inference: The unprompted move is the reporter's observation (S01); the wording is hers and is stable from 2024 to 2025 (S01, S04; a near-identical line in the Broadway.com write-up of S03 is unverified). She names the advantage, does not argue with it, and promises work in return. That pre-emptive acknowledgment of a likely criticism fits Six (anticipating the objection), One (owning what is fair) and Three (managing the image) about equally.
claims.alternative: This is also the answer any publicist would recommend to a famous child debuting in 2024, when 'nepo baby' coverage was at its height. On its own it shows media competence, not motive.

claims.claim: Sarah Paulson, whom Beatty calls 'one of my very best friends in the world' (TODAY, September 2026), told Town & Country in September 2026: 'There is something unnervingly, dazzlingly self-assured about Ella.'
claims.passage: Sarah Paulson, now one of her closest friends, told [Town & Country](https://www.townandcountrymag.com/leisure/arts-and-culture/a73571951/ella-beatty-lizzie-borden-interview-2026/) in September 2026, "There is something unnervingly, dazzlingly self-assured about Ella."
claims.inference: The gap between outer composure and inner report is the most interesting unexplained feature of the record. Composure over private nerves fits a Six who has prepared, a Nine whose calm surface hides inner activity, and a Three whose presentation is polished.
claims.alternative: Paulson is her closest friend; a friend's flattering description in a cover story is not neutral. 'Least interesting person in the room' describes her Feud character's situation as much as her own.

claims.claim: Of landing the Monster lead she told Variety (September 17, 2026): 'When I found out that I had gotten the part, I was over the moon and also really scared.'

claims.inference: The pattern spans three productions and three years. The obligation runs to people (the cast, the writers, a living person) rather than to an abstract standard, and it arrives together with fear ('really scared'). That combination of duty and anxiety is the main support for the Six reading.
claims.alternative: 'Honoring the real person' is stock junket language for any biographical role, and humility about a first lead is expected. A One would also speak of responsibility, though usually of getting it right rather than not letting people down; a Nine would also defer to the authors to avoid imposing herself.

claims.inference: Her answer pairs responsibility to a family legacy with the hope of being judged on her work; it repeats the 2024 Vogue shape (C07).
claims.alternative: Interviewer is her close friend; the answer is also standard media practice for a famous child.

claims.claim: Her handling of the inheritance question is consistent from 2024 to 2025 (name the advantage, don't argue, promise work), and the consistency shows media sense more than motive.
claims.passage: The answer hasn't changed shape since Vogue: name the advantage, don't argue with it, promise work in return. It is also what a publicist would tell any famous child debuting in the 2024 "nepo baby" moment, so it shows media sense more than motive.
claims.inference: Same structure in S01 (February 2024) and S04 (June 2025).
claims.alternative: Could also reflect sincere conviction; the record cannot separate the two.

claims.claim: For Appropriate, Paulson and Michael Esper read with several actresses; Paulson recalls 'when you walked out, Michael and I turned to each other and we're like, "It's got to be Ella Beatty"' and told her 'I had no idea who your parents were.'
claims.passage: For _Appropriate_, Paulson and her co-star Michael Esper read with several actresses. "When you walked out, Michael and I turned to each other and we're like, 'It's got to be Ella Beatty,'" Paulson recalled. She also told her, "I had no idea who your parents were."
claims.inference: Paulson's account in Interview (S04) and Town & Country (S20); Beatty's own version of the dinner on Drew Barrymore ('maybe 6:00 p.m. to, I don't know, 12:30', S18). A second casting by audition, with a lead actor claiming no knowledge of her parents.
claims.alternative: Paulson is now her closest friend and a Monster co-star, so her testimony is affectionate and interested. Town & Country says the dinner was the next night at the Waverly Inn; Beatty says it followed the offer. Minor, compatible discrepancy.

claims.claim: Max Winkler (director of six of eight episodes, executive producer) told ScreenRant that after watching a self-tape from casting director Tiffany Little Canfield he called Ryan Murphy and said 'We got her'; Murphy watched the seven tapes without being told which one and asked 'Is it Ella?'. She had worked with Murphy on Feud.
claims.passage: _Monster_ came from a self-tape. Max Winkler, who directed six of the eight episodes and is an executive producer, told [ScreenRant](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RooR7nJOmiM) that after watching a tape from casting director Tiffany Little Canfield he called Murphy and said, "We got her." Murphy watched all seven tapes without being told which one, then called back and asked, "Is it Ella?" Both men are selling the show, and she had already worked for Murphy on _Feud_, so no one can measure what the name did before the tape. The accounts agree that a tape was required.
claims.inference: Winkler's account (S19, audio re-checked) agrees with Town & Country's report of a self-taped audition (S20); Deadline reported an 'extensive multi-country casting search' (S09). The record shows a tape was required; it cannot measure what the name did before it.
claims.alternative: Winkler and Murphy are interested parties promoting the show, Winkler is himself the son of a famous actor (S20), and a prior working relationship with Murphy plus her name can open the door to an audition. The record cannot measure how much the name helped, only that a tape was required.

claims.claim: On The Drew Barrymore Show (September 2026), responding to Barrymore's own wish to 'honor this family', she said the family profession 'helped me feel a sense of belonging really young. But the older I get, the more I feel that responsibility to kind of carry that torch on.'
claims.passage: She frames the inheritance as belonging and duty. On [_The Drew Barrymore Show_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e8IWMwnMAEE) in September 2026, she agreed with Barrymore's wish to "honor this family" and said the family profession "helped me feel a sense of belonging really young. But the older I get, the more I feel that responsibility to kind of carry that torch on." It is the most Six-flavored vocabulary in the record, though Barrymore supplied the prompt.
claims.inference: Belonging plus responsibility to an inherited group is the most Six-flavored theme in the record; the same 'carry the torch' line appears in 2024 (S03). Audio re-check matched the caption wording.
claims.alternative: She is agreeing with Barrymore's prompt ('I feel a cosmic pull that I want to honor this family'); reverence for famous parents is the safe daytime-TV answer and fits Nine or Two as well.

claims.claim: She told Variety she felt 'a huge responsibility to the part, to the anthology, to the real person' on getting the Monster role.
claims.passage: "I felt a huge responsibility to the part, to the anthology, to the real person," she told Variety.
claims.inference: Part of the same Variety answer as C11; the obligation runs to the work and to people, alongside fear.
claims.alternative: 'Honoring the real person' is stock junket language for a biographical role.

claims.claim: At the September 9, 2026 Netflix press conference (Showbiz Junkies report) she said she felt 'How am I gonna do this and what does it mean?' and that starting work before pre-production helped because 'all of those things that aren't necessarily tangible work can help you feel like you're starting.'
claims.passage: At Netflix's September 9 press conference, [reported by Showbiz Junkies](https://www.showbizjunkies.com/tv/netflix-monster-lizzie-borden-cast-press-conference/), she said she also felt, "How am I gonna do this and what does it mean?" So she started before pre-production, because that work "can help you feel like you're starting."
claims.inference: Consistent across a 2025 stage run and the 2026 series. The same-room contrast with Hall (S14) shows this is her approach, not the production's requirement. Anxiety answered by preparation, reference material and trusted structure is the behavior that most separates a Six reading from a Nine reading, which would predict less nerves and less effort spent securing the ground.
claims.alternative: First-lead nerves are universal; heavy research for a historical role is common; the diary book was the director's own creation, so using it may reflect the production's culture as much as her temperament. A Three would also over-prepare for a career-making role, and a One would research to get it right. All accounts are hers.

claims.claim: She told Collider: 'Right away, when I found out I had the part, I listened to every single podcast and video that's ever been published in the world. I couldn't be stopped if I had a WiFi connection.'
claims.passage: "Right away, when I found out I had the part, I listened to every single podcast and video that's ever been published in the world. I couldn't be stopped if I had a WiFi connection."
claims.inference: Corroborated in a separate junket clip ('I was kind of voracious after I got the part', S16). Preparation as the answer to uncertainty.
claims.alternative: Heavy research for a historical role is common; she then narrowed to 'what was on the page' (S13).

claims.claim: At the same press conference, Rebecca Hall said 'I did absolutely nothing' to prepare and Charlie Hunnam described a couple of days of reading, while Beatty described a book, a movement coach and work before pre-production.
claims.passage: At the same press conference, asked how they had prepared, Rebecca Hall said, "I did absolutely nothing." Charlie Hunnam had spent a couple of days reading. Beatty described a book, a movement coach and work before pre-production. The difference was hers, not the job's.
claims.inference: Same-room contrast in one report (S14) shows her level of preparation was her own choice, not the production's requirement. Hunnam's words in the report are 'a little, you know, couple of days of reading', so the draft paraphrases him.
claims.alternative: Lead actors often prepare more than supporting actors; Hall framed her choice as artistic freedom, not lack of care.

claims.claim: She told Anthony Meindl (February 2025) that before replacing Elle Fanning in Appropriate she had about two days of table work, learned the blocking from a video and the understudies, and 'came in off book, so that would never be an issue'; director Lila Neugebauer told her from the start to find her own version, and 'because I felt that assurance from her going into it, I didn't feel a pressure to replicate anybody else's.'
claims.passage: _Appropriate_ was the same move under more pressure. She told the acting teacher Anthony Meindl on his [_In The Moment_ podcast](https://soundcloud.com/anthonymeindl/anthonyinterviewsellabeatty) in February 2025 that she had about two days of table work before taking over, learned the blocking from a video and the understudies, and "came in off book, so that would never be an issue." The director, Lila Neugebauer, told her from the start to find her own version. "Because I felt that assurance from her going into it, I didn't feel a pressure to replicate anybody else's," Beatty said.
claims.inference: A concrete, consequential episode told twice (S05 at length, S04 briefly: 'I had such an abbreviated rehearsal process... I had to learn on the job'). The sequence is: remove the controllable risk (lines), take permission from the authority in charge, then contribute within the existing structure. That ordering is Six-like; serving the structure is also Nine-like and One-like.
claims.alternative: Learning lines before a put-in is basic professionalism, and directors routinely tell replacements not to imitate. The apology joke is self-deprecating banter. Her account only.

claims.claim: The Appropriate sequence runs: remove the controllable risk, take permission from the authority in charge, then contribute.
claims.passage: First she removed the risk she could control. Then she took permission from the person in charge. Then she brought herself.
claims.inference: Ordering drawn from her own account (C33). Securing ground before contributing is Six-like.
claims.alternative: Serving the existing structure also fits Nine and One; learning lines first is basic professionalism.

claims.claim: During the 2025 run of Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes she said she missed the play on nights off, 'Sometimes we have four or five days between performances and I get really nervous,' and took home director Ian Rickson's 'diary book' of rehearsal images and writings.
claims.passage: On nights off from _Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes_ in 2025, she missed the play. "Sometimes we have four or five days between performances and I get really nervous," she told Paulson, so she took home the director's "diary book" from rehearsals.
claims.inference: The nerves are tied to time away from the play; her remedy is a trusted reference object from the director. Anxiety answered by structure.
claims.alternative: Her stated reason is missing the characters, not fear of failure; the diary book was the director's own creation, so using it reflects his culture as well as her temperament.

claims.claim: She told Town & Country her method as a newcomer: 'I felt the best thing to do was to sit very quietly, watch, and pray, and then work extremely hard and show up off-book.'
claims.passage: Her approach as a newcomer, she told Town & Country, was to "sit very quietly, watch, and pray, and then work extremely hard and show up off-book."
claims.inference: Her own account in 2024 and 2026, corroborated by Jackman's testimony in Town & Country (S20). Preparation and observation are how she manages being new among famous people.
claims.alternative: Conservatory training and ordinary replacement-actor diligence explain much of this, and a famous name raises the cost of being caught unprepared. Jackman co-starred and the production was his company's, so he is an interested party. 'Pray' is a figure of speech, not a religious claim.

claims.claim: Counterevidence: of Appropriate she also said 'I didn't have a lot of time to be scared because I got the job and then we started'; Hugh Jackman told Town & Country she is 'always prepared, kind, funny, and fearless'; Paulson's first impression was 'self-possessed'.
claims.passage: The record pushes back too. Of _Appropriate_, she also told Paulson, "I didn't have a lot of time to be scared because I got the job and then we started." Nerves and over-preparation are ordinary in young actors, and a famous name raises the cost of being caught unprepared. The people who work with her see composure. Jackman told Town & Country she is "always prepared, kind, funny, and fearless." Paulson's word is "self-possessed."
claims.inference: Collaborators see composure, not anxiety; her own account includes a moment of no fear. Weakens the Six reading.
claims.alternative: Jackman and Paulson are friends and collaborators promoting shared work; composure over private nerves is also compatible with Six.

claims.claim: Speaking to Meindl during Ghosts rehearsals (February 2025), she said of the Appropriate takeover: 'part of what was so great about it is that I didn't have time to worry about it... I didn't really have time to get self-conscious or, um, you know, self-involved about it.'
claims.passage: Talking to Meindl during _Ghosts_ rehearsals, she found an upside in the rush of the _Appropriate_ takeover. "Part of what was so great about it is that I didn't have time to worry about it," she said. "I didn't really have time to get self-conscious or, um, you know, self-involved about it."
claims.inference: She experiences being too busy to worry or be self-conscious as relief; this is the half of the answer that precedes C32 and keeps it in context.
claims.alternative: Whisper transcript, no speaker labels; attribution follows the turn (the host asks about the role, she answers). The same answer continues 'so many things to serve and so many people to please' (cited in the Two section as C35).

claims.claim: She described worry as a habit she works against: 'Being present and kind of being where your feet are, it's something I try to try really hard and fail at often frequently to live by... trusting yourself to have, you know, the tools and the ability to handle it when you're faced with it is, um, something I'm still really trying to do. And God knows that was something I did in that play' (of Appropriate, February 2025).
claims.passage: "Being present and kind of being where your feet are, it's something I try to try really hard and fail at often frequently to live by. It's just like, you know, so much of what we worry about in life, so many of the things that we are so, so emotionally fraught about, you know, you can't handle until you're there. And I think trusting yourself to have, you know, the tools and the ability to handle it when you're faced with it is, um, something I'm still really trying to do. And God knows that was something I did in that play."
claims.inference: This is the most specific self-description in the record and the strongest single support for the Six reading: anticipatory worry plus a stated, ongoing effort to trust her own capacity to cope. That is the Six's characteristic growth task. The speed-round lines repeat the theme in a joking register. It is unprompted in the sense that she extends the host's point about tragedy into a statement about herself.
claims.alternative: A single interview with a friend and acting teacher whose theme that day was presence ('In the Moment'); she may be echoing the host's framing. Nine also strives to be 'where your feet are' and could describe the same struggle as getting lost in others' agendas rather than in worry. The speed-round 'Everything. Ghosts.' is a joke riffing on the episode's ghosts theme. Auto-transcribed with Whisper; no speaker labels; attribution follows the conversational turn ('that play' is Appropriate, her show, not the host's). The draft quotes it with 'um' restored and the opening 'and, uh' dropped; the line follows the host's monologue about wasted worry, and 'that play' (Appropriate) and the host's reply 'I'm sorry I missed it' confirm the speaker.

claims.claim: The worry/self-trust passage supports Six (growth task of trusting one's capacity to cope) and Nine (relief at having no room for self).
claims.passage: Read as a Six, that is the type's growth task in her own words: learning to trust that she can handle what she fears before it arrives. Read as a Nine, the telling detail comes first. The rush felt good because it left no room for her.
claims.inference: Both halves of the same answer (C51, C32) are set side by side so neither reading gets only the friendly half.
claims.alternative: May echo the host's theme of presence; a single conversation with a friend.

claims.claim: She describes relief at not being the subject: 'It's a relief to come to work and remember you're being someone else' (Interview, 2025); in 2026 she told Town & Country she has 'a certain amount of discomfort about being a public person' and wants audiences 'thinking about the character and not me', while 'There is also joy in sharing your life with people.'
claims.passage: She keeps describing that relief. "It's a relief to come to work and remember you're being someone else," she told Paulson. In 2026 she told Town & Country she has "a certain amount of discomfort about being a public person" and wants audiences "thinking about the character and not me," while allowing, "There is also joy in sharing your life with people."
claims.inference: Stable across 2024-2026 and three outlets. The weight on not being the subject counts against Three and supports Nine (self-forgetting) or Six (visibility as exposure). She allows that this may 'change and fluctuate with time', so it is a current position.
claims.alternative: She attributes the 'vessel' principle to her training ('What I grew up learning', S01), so it may be a learned craft ideology or family culture rather than temperament. Reticence can also be strategy for an actor whose name already draws attention. She keeps a public Instagram account and does extensive press.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck after her next major press cycle (for example The Bell Jar release or awards season): has her stated comfort with public life changed?

claims.claim: She credits luck: 'I feel like the luckiest lady in the world' (Entertainment Tonight, September 12, 2026, audio re-checked); the same register appears on TODAY ('I can't believe my luck'), at Tribeca and in the 2025 podcast.
claims.passage: Credit runs the same way. "I feel like the luckiest lady in the world," she told [Entertainment Tonight](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DdDLa9vctOA) before the premiere.
claims.inference: The pattern appears in every 2026 interview, including unscripted carpet and morning-show settings, and she volunteers the deflection herself (S20). It argues against an image-first Three reading, which would more often own the result, and fits Nine (self-minimizing), Six (credit to the group and its leaders) and Two (attention on others). The 2025 podcast repeats the register outside a junket: 'I was so lucky. And I was so lucky' (S05, about 24:05-24:13), 'So I'm so lucky. I'm so lucky' (about 47:05).
claims.alternative: This is the expected register for a famous child in nepotism-conscious press and for any newcomer on a junket; publicists coach it. Effusive praise of co-stars ('She's the best', S13) is junket convention. The pattern shows how she presents, not necessarily what she believes.

claims.claim: She told Meindl (February 2025) that she still feels disbelief 'about every project that I've ever done... there's a part of me that feels like, Oh my God, I can't believe they picked me.'
claims.passage: Of every project since, she told Meindl, "there's a part of me that feels like, Oh my God, I can't believe they picked me."
claims.inference: Consistent across an unhurried 52-minute conversation with a friend (S05, about 09:58-10:11 and 34:28-34:47) and a 2026 junket (S08). The expectation of rejection is a habit of mind she describes, not only a polite phrase. It fits Six (anticipating the bad outcome) and Nine (self-discounting) and argues against an achievement-confident Three.
claims.alternative: Surprise at being cast is universal among young actors and is the humble answer a famous child is expected to give. 'Every project' includes jobs she got after auditioning against many others, which makes the surprise plausible as sincere.

claims.claim: Asked by Town & Country how she had changed, she said, 'I'll answer authentically even though I want to deflect.'
claims.passage: Asked by Town & Country how she had changed, she flagged the reflex first. "I'll answer authentically even though I want to deflect," she said.
claims.inference: She names her own deflection reflex, which argues against an image-first Three reading.
claims.alternative: Said 'with a laugh'; a light framing of an ordinary interview move.

claims.claim: Her credit-deflection fits Nine's self-discounting and Six's expectation of the worse outcome, argues against Three, and is also the expected register for a famous child in nepotism-conscious press.
claims.passage: A Three tends to own the result. She hands it to luck and collaborators, and admits the urge to deflect. That fits a Nine's self-discounting and a Six's expectation of the worse outcome. It is also the expected register for a famous child in nepotism-conscious press.
claims.inference: Draws on C14, C31 and C53.
claims.alternative: Publicists coach this register; it shows presentation, not necessarily belief.

claims.claim: She leans on a small circle: of Paulson, 'We call every 15 minutes' and Paulson is 'there for advice at any minute' (TODAY broadcast captions, September 2026); Tom Hollander came to her Feud dressing room privately to offer to run lines (Vogue, 2024); with her mother, 'once a day, debrief' (Drew Barrymore, September 2026, audio re-checked).
claims.passage: When pressure rises, she reaches for a small circle. "We call every 15 minutes," she said of Paulson on [TODAY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q6n83ZQZX2w) in September 2026, a joke with a point. Paulson, she said, is "there for advice at any minute." On _Feud_, Tom Hollander came to her dressing room privately to offer to run lines, and with her mother it's "once a day, debrief," she told [Drew Barrymore](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GYkLldtGQ3s).
claims.inference: Reliance on trusted, experienced people for advice and steadiness is repeated across 2024-2026 and fits the Six's search for reliable support; the speed and warmth of the attachments also fit Two and Nine. Her own stated function for the support system is to keep her grounded and stop her 'head' getting 'too big', which is a check on herself rather than a request for reassurance.
claims.alternative: 'Every 15 minutes' is hyperbole. A 24-26-year-old new to New York theater with famous mentors would plausibly lean on them regardless of type, and several mentors approached her first (Paulson's dinner, Hollander's visit, S20, S01). This is relationship-forming, not proof of anxiety.

claims.claim: She describes auditions as exposure and relies on peers to process them: 'auditioning can be so hard. It can be such a vulnerable, scary thing to do'; 'you don't really know, you know, if you're even kind of accepted in that room yet'; 'it just helps to be able to have a friend to call to be like, Oh my God, that audition was a nightmare. Or I don't know that went well. I don't know what to do with myself'; she credits acting school for giving her 'lots of friends of all ages' to lean on.
claims.passage: She has said what the circle is for, especially around auditions, where "you don't really know, you know, if you're even kind of accepted in that room yet," as she told Meindl. Her remedy is "a friend to call to be like, Oh my God, that audition was a nightmare."
claims.inference: Acceptance and uncertainty are the terms she uses for audition fear, and peer support is her remedy. Together with C16 this shows a consistent strategy: manage uncertainty through trusted company. That is the Six pattern; it is also ordinary actor community talk.
claims.alternative: Responding to the host's story about a client; generic to the profession. In this stretch of the auto-transcript, a line about trying to 'be what you want... beautiful enough for you... interesting enough for you' may be hers or the host's; do not quote it without checking the audio.

claims.claim: Reliance on mentors is ordinary at her age and situation, and several approached her first (Paulson's dinner after the Appropriate offer; Hollander's dressing-room visit).
claims.passage: Leaning on mentors is ordinary at 24 in a new city, and several of hers approached her first.
claims.inference: Counterweight to C16: the circle formed partly at others' initiative.
claims.alternative: Age 24 applies to 2024; she was 23 at the Feud shoot.

claims.claim: Max Winkler told Town & Country: 'There's a wide-eyedness to Ella that can sometimes conceal how devastatingly perceptive she is... She is completely tuned into what everybody else in the room is doing.'
claims.passage: Winkler sees a version of this from the outside. "There's a wide-eyedness to Ella that can sometimes conceal how devastatingly perceptive she is," he told Town & Country. "She is completely tuned into what everybody else in the room is doing."
claims.inference: Two collaborators independently describe attention to others and the load she carried. Being 'tuned into what everybody else in the room is doing' is the trait each live type explains differently: Six as vigilance, Two as attunement to others' needs, Nine as merging with the room, Three as reading the audience.
claims.alternative: Interested party promoting the show; listening to scene partners is also a trained craft value (see C56).

claims.claim: Winkler's observation fits each live type differently, and matches the craft rule she credits to her parents: 'What the other person is doing is always more interesting than what you can create' (TODAY, September 2026).
claims.passage: Each live type can claim that line: a Six scanning the room for safety, a Two for what people need, a Nine merging with it, a Three reading the audience. It is also the craft rule she says her parents taught her. "What the other person is doing is always more interesting than what you can create," she said on TODAY.
claims.inference: The 'listen' rule is cited in 2024 (Vogue, via Gene Hackman and her father) and 2026 (TODAY broadcast captions), so attentiveness may be craft as much as temperament.
claims.alternative: The rule is her report of her parents' advice, not their words.

claims.claim: Six case: across three years she volunteers fear followed by a plan running through preparation and trusted people, and in February 2025 named trusting herself to handle her worries as 'something I'm still really trying to do.'
claims.passage: The Six case is what she volunteers across three years and very different rooms: fear, then a plan that runs through preparation and people she trusts. In February 2025 she named the Six's central work, trusting herself to handle what she worries about, as "something I'm still really trying to do."
claims.inference: Summarizes C11, C12, C46, C33, C49, C16, C34 and C32.
claims.alternative: See C58, C13 and C50.

claims.claim: Against Six: nearly all evidence is self-report in promotional settings, the two longest conversations were with friends, colleagues describe calm, and she shows none of the testing of authority often seen in Sixes.
claims.passage: Against it, nearly all of this is her own account in promotional settings, and the two longest conversations were with friends. Her colleagues describe calm. She also shows none of the testing of authority that often comes with Six.
claims.inference: Mirrors type_hypothesis.against.
claims.alternative: Absence of testing behavior may reflect the promotional record rather than her.

claims.claim: She attaches quickly ('we just kind of fell in love immediately', of Paulson on TODAY, September 2026) and defers to 'what was on the page' (Collider; press conference).
claims.passage: She attaches fast ("we just kind of fell in love immediately," she said of Paulson on TODAY) and defers easily to "what was on the page."
claims.inference: Quick trust and comfortable deference cut against the suspicious, testing side of Six and fit Nine; deference to an authority's structure is also compatible with Six. Used in the draft as evidence against Six.
claims.alternative: Junket etiquette favors praise of colleagues and creators; no account shows her disagreeing with a director.

claims.claim: Nine case: credit to luck and others, relief at being someone else, wish to disappear into roles; her word for work going well is 'available' (Lizzie's sensibility 'felt really available right away', Entertainment Tonight); advice to her younger self, 'Take it a day at a time' (Meindl speed round).
claims.passage: The Nine case is how she presents: credit to luck and others, relief at being someone else, a wish to disappear into roles. Her word for work going well is "available." Lizzie's sensibility "felt really available right away," she told Entertainment Tonight. Her advice to her younger self, she told Meindl: "Take it a day at a time."
claims.inference: Draws on C14, C15 and the 'available' vocabulary (also 'a lot more available on set', Variety, S12).
claims.alternative: 'Available' is common actor shorthand; the speed round is off the cuff.

claims.claim: Against Nine: she names fear and works on it ('I was kind of voracious after I got the part', No Intervals, September 2026, audio re-checked).
claims.passage: What strains it is that Nines tend to turn fear down, and she turns it up and goes to work on it. "I was kind of voracious after I got the part," she told [No Intervals](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZPPP5dTamkM).
claims.inference: A Nine reading predicts less named fear and less effort spent securing the ground.
claims.alternative: Energetic research for a career-making role is common to all types.

claims.claim: Asked by Paulson in 2025 whether she always wanted to be an actor, she said 'Always, always.'
claims.passage: Her ambition is old and plain. Asked by Paulson whether she had always wanted to act, she said, "Always, always."
claims.inference: An old, unambiguous ambition strains the Nine reading's self-forgetting.
claims.alternative: Nearly every actor says this; banter with a friend.

claims.claim: Two case: fast attachments, unstinting praise for collaborators, her job on Monster 'to love and advocate for the person' (Gayety, September 2026), and her imagined alternative of 'teaching theater to really little ones' (Meindl speed round); against it, she is mostly the one looked after and no account shows her giving care or resenting that it goes unnoticed.
claims.passage: The Two case is the warmth: fast attachments, unstinting praise for collaborators, and a job on _Monster_ she described to [Gayety](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kwtu_M-LkBQ) as "to love and advocate for the person." If she weren't acting, she told Meindl, she would be "teaching theater to really little ones." Against it, in this record she is mostly the one being looked after, and no account shows her giving care or resenting that it goes unnoticed.
claims.inference: Her imagined alternative life is in service and connection with children; her stated pleasure in acting is connection with scene partners. This is the main Two-leaning material and also fits Nine's love of shared play.
claims.alternative: Speed-round answers are off the cuff; teaching is a common actor's alternative.

claims.claim: Three case: the fast start, 'Exceptionally poised', the nepotism question handled unprompted, the hope that her work will 'make me separate'; against it, admitted deflection, discomfort with being public, and a self-improvement goal that is moral rather than professional: 'I hope I'm becoming someone who, over time, becomes more conscientious and thoughtful' (Town & Country).
claims.passage: The Three case is the polish: the fast start, "Exceptionally poised," the nepotism question handled before anyone asks, the hope that her work will "make me separate." Against it are the deflection she admits, her discomfort with being public, and a goal that is moral rather than professional: "I hope I'm becoming someone who, over time, becomes more conscientious and thoughtful."

type_hypothesis.against: (1) The people who work with her describe composure, not anxiety: Sarah Paulson's 'self-possessed' and 'unnervingly, dazzlingly self-assured... very open, clear, and confident' (C18), Hugh Jackman's 'fearless' (C10), Max Winkler's calm 'wide-eyedness' (C19). (2) There is no sign of the questioning, testing or suspicion of authority that usually accompanies Six; she trusts quickly ('fell in love immediately' with Paulson, Graynor and Krieps, C06, C16) and defers comfortably to the script and creators (C13). (3) Her relief at 'being someone else' and wish to 'disappear into roles' (C15) fit Nine's self-forgetting at least as well as Six's caution. (4) Every worry statement is self-report, and the two longest interviews are with personal friends (Paulson, S04; the acting teacher Anthony Meindl, S05); stage fright, audition dread and over-preparation are ordinary for any young actor. (5) Nepotism scrutiny supplies a non-type reason for her humility, preparation and pre-emptive acknowledgment of privilege (C07, C10, C14). (6) She also says 'I didn't have a lot of time to be scared' (S04) and enjoys being thrown in (C33), and in February 2025 she described the Ghosts rehearsal phase where 'everything feels bad' without alarm (S05). (7) The entire record is February 2024 to October 2026, almost all of it promotional.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 9 explains much of how she presents: credit always goes to luck and to others (C14, C31); she prefers to be 'a vessel for a character' and finds it 'a relief to come to work and remember you're being someone else' (C15); she merges warmly with collaborators and praises them without reserve (C13, C16, C19); friends see an unruffled, 'least Hollywood' calm (C18); her vocabulary for good work is that it felt 'available', 'easy' and 'fun and easy' (S08, S13, S19); she defers to 'what was on the page' (C13); she recoils from violence and others' pain (S11, S19); she values 'being where your feet are' and would tell her younger self to 'take it a day at a time' (C32). What strains the Nine reading: she names fear readily and repeatedly ('really scared', 'How am I going to do this?', 'really nervous', 'Everything', C11, C12, C32); she answers it with 'voracious' effort and preparation (C12, C33); she says she is 'Not patient by nature' (S15); she seeks frequent advice from a small circle (C16); and her ambition is old and unambiguous ('Always, always', C24, S04). Type 2 is live: relational intensity and quick attachments (C06, C16), unstinting praise, 'so many people to please' in Appropriate (S05), 'my job as the actress was to love and advocate for the person' (S15), her mother's 'Be kind' rule (C09), an imagined alternative life teaching small children (C35), and Winkler's 'completely tuned into what everybody else in the room is doing' (C19); against it, in the record she is mostly the one receiving care and mentorship (Paulson's dinner, Hollander's visit, Graynor), with no account of her helping others or of pride or resentment around giving, and she is uneasy being seen in public (C15). Type 3 is live: an unusually fast, efficient start (C03); polish ('Exceptionally poised', S01); unprompted management of the nepotism question (C07); 'work extremely hard and show up off-book' (C10); and the hope that her work will 'make me separate' (C07); against it, the reflexive credit deflection she herself names ('I want to deflect', C14), discomfort with the public persona and the wish that audiences forget her (C15), and a self-improvement goal that is moral rather than professional ('more conscientious and thoughtful', C25). Types 1 and 4 were tested and set aside for now: One fits the punctuality, earnestness and conscientiousness (C09, C20, C25) but nothing shows an inner critic aimed at standards or irritation with others' errors; Four fits the sensitivity, imagination and being-seen vocabulary (S11, S19, S06, C24) but she rarely frames herself as different and calls herself 'a very normal lady' (C15).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: None that is defensible yet. The best candidate separates Six from Nine: what she does with fear. Across three years and several settings she names anticipatory fear readily (Monster: 'over the moon and also really scared', 'How am I going to do this?'; Sexual Misconduct: 'I get really nervous' between performances; Appropriate: 'so new and scary') and answers it by securing the ground: researching until 'I couldn't be stopped if I had a WiFi connection', starting work before pre-production because it 'can help you feel like you're starting', arriving off book 'so that would never be an issue', taking the director's diary home, calling trusted people, and drawing her freedom from an authority's assurance (C12, C16, C33). In February 2025 she named trusting herself 'to have the tools and the ability to handle it' as something she is 'still really trying to do' (C32), which is the Six's characteristic growth task; a Nine reading predicts less named fear and more settling into the group's flow. But every instance is self-report, the two longest interviews are with friends, and the worries are the ordinary worries of a young actor; the people who work with her describe composure instead (C18, C19). Nothing on record shows her in a conflict, under sustained public criticism, or making a costly choice against the advice of the people she trusts, which is where Six and Nine (and Two and Three) would behave differently. On this record the Six read cannot be held above low confidence, so the profile is an open case.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The gap between her inner report (nervous, scared of 'everything', shy among glamorous people) and the composure everyone around her describes ('unnervingly, dazzlingly self-assured'). Why someone so relational and so warm with collaborators finds it 'a relief' to be someone else at work and has 'a certain amount of discomfort about being a public person'. Whether forgoing child acting was her choice or her parents' rule. How much the family name opened doors that her auditions then closed, which the record cannot measure. Why she took two 2026 roles about daughters and parents (Act One, Monster); she says she will be 'examining that'. How she behaves in a disagreement, under bad reviews, or when the people she trusts disagree with her: no account exists. What she wants for herself beyond 'meaningful work' and 'people that are really curious about the world'.

open_case.reason: Ella Beatty is 26 and under three years into public life: her first professional screen role aired in January 2024, her Broadway debut came that March, and her first lead (Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story) premiered on September 17, 2026. The record is a sequence of promotional cycles (Feud and Appropriate in 2024; Ghosts and Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes in 2025; Act One and Monster in 2026). It holds one long reported profile (Town & Country, September 2026), one 52-minute podcast with a friend who is an acting teacher, a Zoom conversation with Sarah Paulson, and about a dozen 3-to-12-minute junket, carpet and talk-show interviews. Third-party testimony comes only from collaborators and close friends (Paulson, Max Winkler, Hugh Jackman, Charlie Hunnam), all interested; no one who knew her before 2024 has spoken on record, and her parents speak about parenting in general rather than about her. Twenty-four sources were opened (four could not be) and five types tested. The leading read (Six) and its rivals disagree about what her fear, deference and warmth are for, and nothing yet shows her in a conflict, under sustained criticism, or deciding against the people she trusts.
settle_signals: The first time she faces sustained public criticism (a badly reviewed project, or a piece that argues her career was handed to her): does she talk about doubting herself, leaning on the people she trusts and preparing harder (Six); shrug it off and keep things smooth without engaging (Nine); focus on how collaborators or audiences were affected (Two); or defend the work and point to results (Three)?

Her first on-record account of a creative disagreement with a director, writer or co-star (none exists as of October 18, 2026): does she describe testing whether she could trust the person before committing (Six), going along until it felt 'available' (Nine), protecting the relationship above the outcome (Two), or doing whatever made the performance land best (Three)?

Awards-season and The Bell Jar press (Golden Globe nominations are due in December 2026; The Bell Jar has wrapped with no release date): does her register stay on luck and gratitude (Nine or Six) or shift toward owning the work (Three), and do nerves and self-trust remain her theme when she is no longer new (Six)?

Her next two or three choices of project: does she return to trusted collaborators and familiar circles, such as Ryan Murphy's company or Sarah Paulson (Six); drift toward whatever comes, with no visible plan (Nine); choose projects for the people involved and the chance to support them (Two); or make a deliberate climb toward bigger and more visible leads (Three)?

The first on-record testimony from someone who knew her before 2024 (a Juilliard classmate or teacher, a Buckley schoolmate, a summer-camp director) describing her under pressure or in a disagreement: do they recall worry and preparation, calm accommodation, caretaking, or drive?
